questions.q: Where do data quality checks typically belong in the medallion flow?
options: At the silver boundary — after casting and deduplication, but before the data is treated as trustworthy enough for gold
In bronze, before any data is ingested at all
Only in gold, after aggregation is already complete
Quality checks don't belong anywhere in medallion architecture
questions.explain: Bronze deliberately keeps everything, including bad rows, so nothing is lost before it's even inspected.

questions.q: What is a quarantine table, and what problem does it solve?
options: A table that keeps bad rows somewhere real and inspectable — a third option beyond Lesson 51's binary drop-or-fill choice
A backup copy of the entire bronze table
A table that automatically fixes bad rows using machine learning
A synonym for the _delta_log transaction history
questions.explain: Nothing is silently discarded, and nothing bad reaches gold either — someone can review it later.

questions.q: Why is a quality metrics table considered a small gold table?
options: It's an aggregate built for one specific question — is data quality getting better or worse over time — exactly matching gold's purpose
It contains the exact same rows as the main gold.daily_revenue table
It's actually stored in the silver layer, not gold
It has no relationship to gold's typical structure
questions.explain: A sudden spike in a bad-row count is an early warning worth investigating, just like any other gold aggregate.

questions.q: Why are "the pipeline ran successfully" and "the data is trustworthy" different claims?
options: A job's Succeeded status only means the code executed without an exception — it says nothing about whether the data itself was actually good
They are always the same claim; a successful run guarantees good data
Job success can only be measured by checking the quarantine table
Data quality can only be assessed by re-running the entire pipeline
questions.explain: Quarantine counts and quality metrics are what actually answer the data-trustworthiness question.

questions.q: How does quarantining differ from Lesson 51's na.drop() or na.fill() approaches?
options: It keeps the bad row somewhere inspectable instead of either losing it entirely or guessing a replacement value
It's functionally identical to na.drop()
It's functionally identical to na.fill()
Quarantining requires deleting the row from bronze as well
questions.explain: This gives someone the ability to review what went wrong upstream, rather than losing the information.
